statements.quote: Before an AI can “calculate” a word, it must chop the text into pieces.
This process is called **Tokenization**.
Depending on how you chop, the AI “sees” the world differently.
Simple Splitting Word-Level
The most intuitive way: Every time there is a space, comma, dot etc., we create a new token.
Before modern subword methods, word-level splitting was the default for systems like the original **IBM Alignment Models** in the early 1990s.

While \citeauthor{zipf1949human} (\citeyear{zipf1949human}) formalized the distribution problem, it was these early translation models that hit the “Out-of-Vocabulary” (OOV) wall, leading researchers to realize that treating “brave” and “bravely” as two completely unrelated IDs was inefficient.
Here, we don't care about words.
We just take every X characters (e.g., Trigrams).
This approach of using chains of dependencies was first pioneered by \citeauthor{markov1913ngram} in \citeyear{markov1913ngram} to describe the statistical structure of language.
Character-Level The Raw View
This treats every single letter and space as its own token.
This is the most granular way to see text.

The concept of viewing text as a sequence of raw characters dates back to \citeauthor{markov1913ngram} (\citeyear{markov1913ngram}), who used it to analyze the statistical structure of Russian literature.

In the era of Deep Learning, the “raw view” was revitalized by \citeauthor{sutskever2011generating} in their paper \citetitle{sutskever2011generating}, which proved that Recurrent Neural Networks could learn to predict the next character with enough precision to form coherent words and sentences from scratch.

WordPiece is a subword method closely related to BPE, but instead of merging the most *frequent* pair, it greedily merges the pair whose combination most improves the **likelihood of the training data**.

The original formulation (Schuster & Nakajima 2012), introduced to handle the massive character sets of Japanese and Korean, optimizes that likelihood directly through an iterative procedure, it has no closed-form per-pair score.
The ratio shown below is a separate, simpler *approximation* used by BERT-style implementations, not the original objective.
WordPiece later became famous as the tokenizer behind Google's **BERT**.
Continuation fragments are marked with `##` (e.g., “tokenization” → `token`, `##iza`, `##tion`).
GPT-style models use BPE instead because byte-level BPE is simpler to train at scale and guarantees coverage of any input without needing an unknown-token fallback.
Initialize the vocabulary with every character present in the training data.

Score every candidate pair , but instead of raw frequency, WordPiece is *defined* as merging the pair that most increases the likelihood of the training data (the original formulation of Schuster & Nakajima 2012).

That likelihood-based objective is not equivalent to a closed-form pair score, so implementations use an approximation: BERT-style tokenizers score each candidate pair with a likelihood-ratio measure:

This closed-form ratio is a *simplification*, not the original formulation, it favors merging pairs whose co-occurrence is high relative to how often each piece appears independently, which is why the formula is a *ratio* rather than a raw frequency: BPE uses raw frequency, BERT-style WordPiece uses the ratio.
Merge the highest-scoring pair and add the new symbol to the vocabulary.
Repeat until the desired vocabulary size is reached.

Tokenize new text using a greedy longest-match-first approach: scan from the beginning of each word, find the longest substring that exists in the vocabulary, emit it, then continue with the remainder.
Continuation fragments are prefixed with (e.g., → , , ).
Sub-word Units The ChatGPT Way
Modern AIs use **BPE (Byte-Pair Encoding)**.
It keeps common words whole but splits rare words into known building blocks like `ing` or `ly`.
The history of BPE is a classic case of an algorithm being repurposed for a new era.
Originally, \citeauthor{gage1994bpe} (\citeyear{gage1994bpe}) developed the technique strictly for data compression, using iterative byte-pair replacement to shrink files.
It remained a niche compression tool until \citeauthor{sennrich2016subword} (\citeyear{sennrich2016subword}) adapted the logic into a subword tokenization strategy.

This shift allowed modern models to handle rare words by breaking them into frequent fragments, effectively solving the “Out-of-Vocabulary” problem that had previously limited word-level neural networks.
Initialize the vocabulary with every individual character (or byte) that appears in the training corpus.
Count all adjacent symbol pairs across the corpus.
For example, in a corpus containing “car” (5×) and “cable” (3×), the pair c a appears 8 times total.
Merge the most frequent pair into a single new symbol and add it to the vocabulary.
This is the core step: BPE always picks the pair with the highest frequency .
Repeat steps 2–3 for a fixed number of merge operations (a hyperparameter).
Each round creates a slightly larger subword unit.
Tokenize new text by applying the learned merge rules in order.
Common words end up as single tokens; rare words get split into known subword fragments (e.g., → + ), effectively solving the Out-of-Vocabulary problem.
🍓 Why LLMs Can't Count Letters
Type a word like **“strawberry”** below and watch how BPE splits it.
The model never sees individual letters, it sees whatever fragments the tokenizer produced during training.
The first part of this chapter showed you the *mechanism*: how a stream of characters is chopped into a fixed vocabulary of subwords so a discrete, finite model can process open-ended text.
statements.section: The Consequence: Tokenization as a Bias

statements.quote: This second part is the *consequence* of that mechanism — the part that is easy to miss because it is invisible in a single-language demo.
statements.section: The Consequence: Tokenization as a Bias

statements.quote: A tokenizer is not a neutral preprocessing step.
statements.section: The Consequence: Tokenization as a Bias

statements.quote: It is a **bias**, baked into the model before a single weight is trained, and it prices every language differently.
statements.section: The Consequence: Tokenization as a Bias

statements.quote: Two of the most consequential, least-discussed properties of a modern LLM — why it costs more to speak in one language than another, and why it sometimes fails in exactly the ways the Strawberry demo above hinted at — live here.
statements.section: The Consequence: Tokenization as a Bias

statements.quote: Building a vocabulary is a decision, not a default.
statements.section: The choices that were never obvious

statements.quote: The options form a spectrum, and each one optimizes a different trade-off:
statements.section: The choices that were never obvious

statements.quote: Moving from word-level to byte-level trades vocabulary size for robustness: the finer the unit, the smaller the vocabulary and the fewer the "cannot be represented" cases.
statements.section: The choices that were never obvious

statements.quote: These are not interchangeable.
statements.section: The choices that were never obvious

statements.quote: What each optimizes — vocabulary size, robustness to unseen input, per-language efficiency — is a choice that the training corpus makes *for you*, usually without you noticing.
statements.section: The choices that were never obvious

statements.quote: Here is the property that matters.
statements.section: The pathology: token inflation

statements.quote: A tokenizer trained mostly on one language builds a vocabulary that is *efficient* for that language and *inefficient* for others.
statements.section: The pathology: token inflation

statements.quote: A subword is a token; the model charges you one token of compute, one slot of context window, and one unit of API cost for each one.
statements.section: The pathology: token inflation

statements.quote: And the *same meaning* does not cost the same number of tokens in every language.
statements.section: The pathology: token inflation

statements.quote: A word that is a single high-frequency subword in the dominant language may need several tokens in another — because its characters, syllables, or words were never frequent enough in the training corpus to be merged into a single subword.
statements.section: The pathology: token inflation

statements.quote: For many lower-resource and non-Latin scripts (Thai, Devanagari, Cyrillic, and a long tail of others) the result is routinely **several times more tokens per word** than English, a disparity now measured and analyzed as a form of infrastructure bias in its own right (\cite[Teklehaymanot & Nejdl, 2025]{tokenbias2025}).
statements.section: The pathology: token inflation

statements.quote: The same sentence, translated faithfully, is *longer* in the low-resource language at the token layer — even though it says the same thing.
statements.section: The pathology: token inflation

statements.quote: This is not a bug in the model; it is a property of the *tokenizer*, fixed before training.
statements.section: The pathology: token inflation

statements.quote: And it compounds in three places at once:
statements.section: The pathology: token inflation

statements.quote: **Cost.** Tokens are billed per token.
statements.section: The pathology: token inflation

statements.quote: A conversation that runs 3–5× longer in tokens costs 3–5× more API money, for an equal amount of meaning.
statements.section: The pathology: token inflation

statements.quote: **Context.** The context window is measured in tokens.
statements.section: The pathology: token inflation

statements.quote: A longer tokenization means the same document *fills the window sooner*, so the model sees less of it — a silent, per-language reduction in effective context.
statements.section: The pathology: token inflation

statements.quote: **Capacity.** The model's attention has a fixed token budget per sequence.
statements.section: The pathology: token inflation

statements.quote: A language that spends more tokens per word gets *fewer words of attention* for the same budget.
statements.section: The pathology: token inflation

statements.quote: > Language is priced by the tokenizer.
statements.section: The pathology: token inflation

statements.quote: The model's competence in a given language is, partly, a function of how *cheap* that language is in tokens — a quantity decided by a vocabulary trained on a corpus that was, in practice, not that language.
statements.section: The pathology: token inflation

statements.quote: Token inflation is a *quantitative* failure: the pieces are real, there are simply too many of them.
statements.section: When the vocabulary is a graveyard: glitch tokens

statements.quote: There is also a stranger, *qualitative* failure.
statements.section: When the vocabulary is a graveyard: glitch tokens

statements.quote: Sometimes a string becomes a single token during tokenizer training, but the model itself almost never sees that token during pretraining.
statements.section: When the vocabulary is a graveyard: glitch tokens

statements.quote: The token exists in the vocabulary, it has an ID, an embedding row, and a place in every weight matrix, but its parameters are barely trained.
statements.section: When the vocabulary is a graveyard: glitch tokens

statements.quote: The result is a **glitch token**: an input the tokenizer handles perfectly and the model has no learned meaning for.
statements.section: When the vocabulary is a graveyard: glitch tokens

statements.quote: The canonical examples come from the GPT-2/GPT-3 tokenizer (the `·` below marks a leading space).
statements.section: When the vocabulary is a graveyard: glitch tokens

statements.quote: In 2023, \citeauthor{rumbelow2023solidgold} collected strings such as `·SolidGoldMagikarp`, `·petertodd`, and `·externalToEVA` that produced bizarre, evasive, or repetitive behavior when used as prompts, including failures to repeat or spell the string back (\cite[Rumbelow & Watkins, 2023]{rumbelow2023solidgold}).
statements.section: When the vocabulary is a graveyard: glitch tokens

statements.quote: The likely cause is a mismatch between the corpus used to *train the tokenizer* and the corpus used to *train the model*: a token can be frequent in the tokenizer's corpus (usernames, code handles, scraped strings) and absent from the model's training data, leaving its embedding close to its random initialization.
statements.section: When the vocabulary is a graveyard: glitch tokens

statements.quote: Glitch tokens are the extreme end of a continuum, not a handful of curiosities.
statements.section: When the vocabulary is a graveyard: glitch tokens

statements.quote: \cite[Land & Bartolo (2024)]{land2024fishing} showed that undertrained tokens are widespread and can be found automatically by comparing a token's frequency in the tokenizer corpus with its exposure in the model.
statements.section: When the vocabulary is a graveyard: glitch tokens

statements.quote: \cite[Li et al. (2024)]{glitchtokens} built a taxonomy and detection pipeline for them, and \cite[Zhang et al. (2024)]{glitchprober2024} extended detection and mitigation.
statements.section: When the vocabulary is a graveyard: glitch tokens

statements.quote: The practical lesson is not “avoid one weird string”; it is that **a vocabulary entry is not a learned concept**.
statements.section: When the vocabulary is a graveyard: glitch tokens

statements.quote: The documented examples are mostly ordinary-looking strings.
statements.section: When the vocabulary is a graveyard: glitch tokens

statements.quote: That is the point: nothing in the surface form tells you whether the token was trained.
statements.section: When the vocabulary is a graveyard: glitch tokens

statements.quote: | Token (the `·` marks a leading space) | What was reported | What it reveals |
statements.section: When the vocabulary is a graveyard: glitch tokens

statements.quote: | `·SolidGoldMagikarp` | Refusals, repetitions, and confusion when asked to repeat or spell it | A token can exist without a usable embedding |
statements.section: When the vocabulary is a graveyard: glitch tokens

statements.quote: | `·petertodd` | Bizarre associations and unstable completions | The model may pattern-match the *string's* scraped context, not its meaning |
statements.section: When the vocabulary is a graveyard: glitch tokens

statements.quote: | `·externalToEVA` | Evasive or malformed answers | Code identifiers can become tokens the language model never learned |
statements.section: When the vocabulary is a graveyard: glitch tokens

statements.quote: | `·davidjl` | Unstable, sometimes evasive behavior | A username can be a single token and a blind spot |
statements.section: When the vocabulary is a graveyard: glitch tokens

statements.quote: | `·RandomRedditor` | Unstable completions | A scraped username can occupy a whole vocabulary slot |
statements.section: When the vocabulary is a graveyard: glitch tokens

statements.quote: | `·repmovsb` | Unstable or evasive behavior | An assembly mnemonic can be a token with no learned semantics |
statements.section: When the vocabulary is a graveyard: glitch tokens

statements.quote: | `·TheNitromeFan` | Repeated or confused output | A fandom handle can be a token the model never learned |
statements.section: When the vocabulary is a graveyard: glitch tokens

statements.quote: The families are recognizable in hindsight: Reddit usernames, UI identifiers such as `·guiActive`, code mnemonics such as `·repmovsb`, and ordinary-looking words such as `·Scaled`.
statements.section: When the vocabulary is a graveyard: glitch tokens

statements.quote: The pattern is general: **the tokenizer's training corpus and the model's training corpus are not the same corpus.** A tokenizer can create a token for a string that is frequent in its own data and then hand the model an embedding row that almost never receives a gradient.
statements.section: When the vocabulary is a graveyard: glitch tokens

statements.quote: The model cannot tell you what the token means, because it was never taught.
statements.section: When the vocabulary is a graveyard: glitch tokens

statements.quote: This is also a security property.
statements.section: When the vocabulary is a graveyard: glitch tokens

statements.quote: A token the model handles unpredictably is a potential bypass: adversarial tokenization can change a model's behavior or slip text past a classifier that segments it differently (\cite[Geh et al., 2025]{geh2025adversarialtokenization}; \cite[Schulz et al., 2025]{tokenbreak2025}).
statements.section: When the vocabulary is a graveyard: glitch tokens

statements.quote: The lesson for anyone deploying a model is dull but important: **test the tokenizer, not just the model**, and treat “this string is one token” as a claim to verify rather than a guarantee.
statements.section: When the vocabulary is a graveyard: glitch tokens

statements.quote: Byte-level BPE \cite[Radford et al., GPT-2 (2019)]{gpt2} solved the *worst* failure — a token the model cannot even *represent*.
statements.section: Byte-level: the floor, not the fix

statements.quote: Because the alphabet is all 256 bytes, every possible input has a tokenization; there is no unknown token, no "cannot read this script." That is a genuine, large win: a byte-level model can, in principle, read *any* language, including ones it was barely trained on.
statements.section: Byte-level: the floor, not the fix

statements.quote: But byte-level does **not** remove the inflation — it only removes the *failure to represent it*.
statements.section: Byte-level: the floor, not the fix

statements.quote: A Thai sentence is still more bytes (hence more tokens) than the same sentence in English, because the information is denser per character in a script with a large alphabet.
statements.section: Byte-level: the floor, not the fix

statements.quote: Byte-level is the **floor**: it guarantees you can tokenize anything.
statements.section: Byte-level: the floor, not the fix

statements.quote: The *relative* cost between languages remains, because it is a property of the languages themselves (how much information per byte), not of the tokenizer's vocabulary.
statements.section: Byte-level: the floor, not the fix

statements.quote: The current research direction is to shrink, or remove, the discrete-token bottleneck altogether.
statements.section: The frontier: removing the discrete bottleneck

statements.quote: The clearest first step is **byte-to-byte** pretraining: model over raw bytes rather than over a hand-built subword vocabulary, so there is no per-language vocabulary to be biased by \cite[Xue et al., ByT5 (2022)]{byt52022}.
statements.section: The frontier: removing the discrete bottleneck

statements.quote: Beyond that, the 2025–26 frontier explores **byte-latent / continuous** representations — learning a continuous "pre-token" space the model predicts over, sidestepping the fixed 256-byte (or fixed-vocabulary) discretization.
statements.section: The frontier: removing the discrete bottleneck

statements.quote: Whether that actually closes the per-language gap, or merely moves the bias into the continuous representation, is an open question; the honest statement is that the *idea* — stop making a fixed vocabulary the unit of thought — is live and consequential, even where the named systems are not yet settled into stable references you can cite.
statements.section: The frontier: removing the discrete bottleneck

statements.quote: The practical takeaway does not depend on the frontier.
statements.section: The frontier: removing the discrete bottleneck

statements.quote: A tokenizer is a **decision with economic and fairness consequences**, not a detail.
statements.section: The frontier: removing the discrete bottleneck

statements.quote: If you deploy a model multilingually, the question "how many tokens does a sentence in language *L* cost, relative to the dominant language?" is a real number, it is not one, and it should be measured — because the model's *effective* context window, and its *price*, are different for every language it serves.
statements.section: The frontier: removing the discrete bottleneck

statements.quote: Glitch tokens are one member of a family.
statements.section: The rest of the bestiary

statements.quote: Once you look at text as *tokens* rather than characters, several other failure modes become visible.
statements.section: The rest of the bestiary

statements.quote: None of them is exotic; all of them are consequences of the same decision to cut text at statistically convenient boundaries.
statements.section: The rest of the bestiary

statements.quote: A number is a sequence of digits; a tokenizer sees a string and may group it in ways that depend on frequency rather than place value.
statements.section: Numbers do not survive the trip

statements.quote: `1234` may be one token while `1235` becomes `123` + `5`; a decimal point, a leading zero, or a thousands separator can change the segmentation again.
statements.section: Numbers do not survive the trip

statements.quote: The model then has to do arithmetic across pieces that do not line up with the digits, which is one reason arithmetic accuracy depends on *how the number was written* (\cite[Singh & Strouse, 2024]{singh2024tokenizationcounts}).
statements.section: Numbers do not survive the trip

statements.quote: The fix is not “train harder”; it is to choose a representation that preserves the structure, for example digit-wise tokenization or an external calculator.
statements.section: Numbers do not survive the trip

statements.quote: Leading and trailing spaces belong to tokens.
statements.section: A space is not nothing

statements.quote: A prompt ending in `The answer is` and one ending in `The answer is ` can have different next-token distributions, because the final token is different.
statements.section: A space is not nothing

statements.quote: This matters most at the boundary between a prompt and a generated continuation, where a partial token can force the model into an awkward segmentation.
statements.section: A space is not nothing

statements.quote: Recent work shows that models can often recover from *non-canonical* tokenizations, but the distribution shift is real and measurable (\cite[Zheng et al., 2025]{zheng2025brokentokens}).
statements.section: A space is not nothing

statements.quote: Boundary-aware prompting and token healing exist precisely to avoid handing the model a split it did not expect.
statements.section: A space is not nothing

statements.quote: Unicode is not a one-to-one mapping from what you see to what the tokenizer receives.
statements.section: One visible character, many tokens

statements.quote: The same visible `é` can be one code point or `e` plus a combining acute accent; an emoji can be a single code point or a zero-width-joiner sequence of several; flags, family emoji, and right-to-left text add more cases.
statements.section: One visible character, many tokens

statements.quote: Normalization forms (NFC, NFD) can therefore change the token sequence without changing the rendered text (\cite[Unicode Consortium, UAX #15]{unicodeuax15}).
statements.section: One visible character, many tokens

statements.quote: Normalize before comparing, classifying, or hashing text — and remember that normalization is itself a lossy decision when the exact byte sequence matters.
statements.section: One visible character, many tokens

statements.quote: Token IDs are not portable.
statements.section: The same string, a different tokenizer

statements.quote: Each model family has its own vocabulary and merge rules, so the same sentence can be longer, shorter, or split at completely different places under a different tokenizer.
statements.section: The same string, a different tokenizer

statements.quote: That is why swapping a tokenizer invalidates the embedding matrix, why token counts from one model are not a budget for another, and why “the context window is 128k tokens” is a statement about a *particular* tokenizer.
statements.section: The same string, a different tokenizer

statements.quote: The tokenizer is part of the model contract, not a preprocessing detail you can change later.
statements.section: The same string, a different tokenizer

statements.quote: If a safety filter and a generator tokenize the same text differently, an attacker can exploit the gap: invisible characters, Cyrillic letters that look Latin, leetspeak, or deliberate segmentation can change one side's view while leaving the other's meaning intact.
statements.section: Spelling, homoglyphs, and filter evasion

statements.quote: This is the practical face of adversarial tokenization (\cite[Geh et al., 2025]{geh2025adversarialtokenization}; \cite[Schulz et al., 2025]{tokenbreak2025}).
statements.section: Spelling, homoglyphs, and filter evasion

statements.quote: Defenses have to normalize and tokenize consistently across every component in the pipeline; a filter that reads characters while the model reads tokens is not protecting the same input.
statements.section: Spelling, homoglyphs, and filter evasion

statements.quote: The pathologies above point to a short engineering checklist:
statements.section: What to do about it

statements.quote: > A tokenizer is a lossy interface between text and thought.
statements.section: What to do about it

statements.quote: The loss is not random: it is a set of decisions about which distinctions matter, made before the model sees a single example.
statements.section: What to do about it

statements.quote: The next time a model “can't count,” “can't spell,” or “goes weird” on an ordinary-looking string, ask the tokenizer first.
statements.section: What to do about it

statements.quote: It is often the part of the system that made the decision, and the part nobody debugged.
statements.section: What to do about it

That likelihood-based objective is not equivalent to a closed-form pair score, so implementations use an approximation: BERT-style tokenizers score each candidate pair with a likelihood-ratio measure:

This closed-form ratio is a *simplification*, not the original formulation, it favors merging pairs whose co-occurrence is high relative to how often each piece appears independently, which is why the formula is a *ratio* rather than a raw frequency: BPE uses raw frequency, BERT-style WordPiece uses the ratio.
Merge the highest-scoring pair and add the new symbol to the vocabulary.
Repeat until the desired vocabulary size is reached.

Tokenize new text using a greedy longest-match-first approach: scan from the beginning of each word, find the longest substring that exists in the vocabulary, emit it, then continue with the remainder. Continuation fragments are prefixed with (e.g., → , , ).
Sub-word Units The ChatGPT Way
Modern AIs use **BPE (Byte-Pair Encoding)**. It keeps common words whole but splits rare words into known building blocks like `ing` or `ly`.

The history of BPE is a classic case of an algorithm being repurposed for a new era. Originally, \citeauthor{gage1994bpe} (\citeyear{gage1994bpe}) developed the technique strictly for data compression, using iterative byte-pair replacement to shrink files. It remained a niche compression tool until \citeauthor{sennrich2016subword} (\citeyear{sennrich2016subword}) adapted the logic into a subword tokenization strategy. This shift allowed modern models to handle rare words by breaking them into frequent fragments, effectively solving the “Out-of-Vocabulary” problem that had previously limited word-level neural networks.
Initialize the vocabulary with every individual character (or byte) that appears in the training corpus.
Count all adjacent symbol pairs across the corpus. For example, in a corpus containing “car” (5×) and “cable” (3×), the pair c a appears 8 times total.
Merge the most frequent pair into a single new symbol and add it to the vocabulary. This is the core step: BPE always picks the pair with the highest frequency .
Repeat steps 2–3 for a fixed number of merge operations (a hyperparameter). Each round creates a slightly larger subword unit.

Tokenize new text by applying the learned merge rules in order. Common words end up as single tokens; rare words get split into known subword fragments (e.g., → + ), effectively solving the Out-of-Vocabulary problem.
🍓 Why LLMs Can't Count Letters
Type a word like **“strawberry”** below and watch how BPE splits it. The model never sees individual letters, it sees whatever fragments the tokenizer produced during training.
The Consequence: Tokenization as a Bias
blocks.section: The Consequence: Tokenization as a Bias

blocks.quote: The first part of this chapter showed you the *mechanism*: how a stream of characters is chopped into a fixed vocabulary of subwords so a discrete, finite model can process open-ended text. This second part is the *consequence* of that mechanism — the part that is easy to miss because it is invisible in a single-language demo. A tokenizer is not a neutral preprocessing step. It is a **bias**, baked into the model before a single weight is trained, and it prices every language differently. Two of the most consequential, least-discussed properties of a modern LLM — why it costs more to speak in one language than another, and why it sometimes fails in exactly the ways the Strawberry demo above hinted at — live here.
blocks.section: The Consequence: Tokenization as a Bias

blocks.quote: The choices that were never obvious
blocks.section: The choices that were never obvious

blocks.quote: Building a vocabulary is a decision, not a default. The options form a spectrum, and each one optimizes a different trade-off:
blocks.section: The choices that were never obvious

blocks.section: The choices that were never obvious

blocks.quote: The subword spectrum. Moving from word-level to byte-level trades vocabulary size for robustness: the finer the unit, the smaller the vocabulary and the fewer the "cannot be represented" cases.
blocks.section: The choices that were never obvious

blocks.quote: These are not interchangeable. What each optimizes — vocabulary size, robustness to unseen input, per-language efficiency — is a choice that the training corpus makes *for you*, usually without you noticing.
blocks.section: The choices that were never obvious

blocks.quote: The pathology: token inflation
blocks.section: The pathology: token inflation

blocks.quote: Here is the property that matters. A tokenizer trained mostly on one language builds a vocabulary that is *efficient* for that language and *inefficient* for others. A subword is a token; the model charges you one token of compute, one slot of context window, and one unit of API cost for each one. And the *same meaning* does not cost the same number of tokens in every language.
blocks.section: The pathology: token inflation

blocks.quote: A word that is a single high-frequency subword in the dominant language may need several tokens in another — because its characters, syllables, or words were never frequent enough in the training corpus to be merged into a single subword. For many lower-resource and non-Latin scripts (Thai, Devanagari, Cyrillic, and a long tail of others) the result is routinely **several times more tokens per word** than English, a disparity now measured and analyzed as a form of infrastructure bias in its own right (\cite[Teklehaymanot & Nejdl, 2025]{tokenbias2025}). The same sentence, translated faithfully, is *longer* in the low-resource language at the token layer — even though it says the same thing.
blocks.section: The pathology: token inflation

blocks.quote: This is not a bug in the model; it is a property of the *tokenizer*, fixed before training. And it compounds in three places at once:
blocks.section: The pathology: token inflation

blocks.quote: 1. **Cost.** Tokens are billed per token. A conversation that runs 3–5× longer in tokens costs 3–5× more API money, for an equal amount of meaning.
blocks.section: The pathology: token inflation

blocks.quote: 2. **Context.** The context window is measured in tokens. A longer tokenization means the same document *fills the window sooner*, so the model sees less of it — a silent, per-language reduction in effective context.
blocks.section: The pathology: token inflation

blocks.quote: 3. **Capacity.** The model's attention has a fixed token budget per sequence. A language that spends more tokens per word gets *fewer words of attention* for the same budget.
blocks.section: The pathology: token inflation

blocks.quote: > Language is priced by the tokenizer. The model's competence in a given language is, partly, a function of how *cheap* that language is in tokens — a quantity decided by a vocabulary trained on a corpus that was, in practice, not that language.
blocks.section: The pathology: token inflation

blocks.quote: When the vocabulary is a graveyard: glitch tokens
blocks.section: When the vocabulary is a graveyard: glitch tokens

blocks.quote: Token inflation is a *quantitative* failure: the pieces are real, there are simply too many of them. There is also a stranger, *qualitative* failure. Sometimes a string becomes a single token during tokenizer training, but the model itself almost never sees that token during pretraining. The token exists in the vocabulary, it has an ID, an embedding row, and a place in every weight matrix, but its parameters are barely trained. The result is a **glitch token**: an input the tokenizer handles perfectly and the model has no learned meaning for.
blocks.section: When the vocabulary is a graveyard: glitch tokens

blocks.quote: The canonical examples come from the GPT-2/GPT-3 tokenizer (the `·` below marks a leading space). In 2023, \citeauthor{rumbelow2023solidgold} collected strings such as `·SolidGoldMagikarp`, `·petertodd`, and `·externalToEVA` that produced bizarre, evasive, or repetitive behavior when used as prompts, including failures to repeat or spell the string back (\cite[Rumbelow & Watkins, 2023]{rumbelow2023solidgold}). The likely cause is a mismatch between the corpus used to *train the tokenizer* and the corpus used to *train the model*: a token can be frequent in the tokenizer's corpus (usernames, code handles, scraped strings) and absent from the model's training data, leaving its embedding close to its random initialization.
blocks.section: When the vocabulary is a graveyard: glitch tokens

blocks.quote: Glitch tokens are the extreme end of a continuum, not a handful of curiosities. \cite[Land & Bartolo (2024)]{land2024fishing} showed that undertrained tokens are widespread and can be found automatically by comparing a token's frequency in the tokenizer corpus with its exposure in the model. \cite[Li et al. (2024)]{glitchtokens} built a taxonomy and detection pipeline for them, and \cite[Zhang et al. (2024)]{glitchprober2024} extended detection and mitigation. The practical lesson is not “avoid one weird string”; it is that **a vocabulary entry is not a learned concept**.
blocks.section: When the vocabulary is a graveyard: glitch tokens

blocks.quote: The documented examples are mostly ordinary-looking strings. That is the point: nothing in the surface form tells you whether the token was trained.
blocks.section: When the vocabulary is a graveyard: glitch tokens

blocks.quote: | Token (the `·` marks a leading space) | What was reported | What it reveals |
blocks.section: When the vocabulary is a graveyard: glitch tokens

blocks.quote: | `·SolidGoldMagikarp` | Refusals, repetitions, and confusion when asked to repeat or spell it | A token can exist without a usable embedding |
blocks.section: When the vocabulary is a graveyard: glitch tokens

blocks.quote: | `·petertodd` | Bizarre associations and unstable completions | The model may pattern-match the *string's* scraped context, not its meaning |
blocks.section: When the vocabulary is a graveyard: glitch tokens

blocks.quote: | `·externalToEVA` | Evasive or malformed answers | Code identifiers can become tokens the language model never learned |
blocks.section: When the vocabulary is a graveyard: glitch tokens

blocks.quote: | `·davidjl` | Unstable, sometimes evasive behavior | A username can be a single token and a blind spot |
blocks.section: When the vocabulary is a graveyard: glitch tokens

blocks.section: When the vocabulary is a graveyard: glitch tokens

blocks.quote: | `·repmovsb` | Unstable or evasive behavior | An assembly mnemonic can be a token with no learned semantics |
blocks.section: When the vocabulary is a graveyard: glitch tokens

blocks.section: When the vocabulary is a graveyard: glitch tokens

blocks.quote: The families are recognizable in hindsight: Reddit usernames, UI identifiers such as `·guiActive`, code mnemonics such as `·repmovsb`, and ordinary-looking words such as `·Scaled`. The pattern is general: **the tokenizer's training corpus and the model's training corpus are not the same corpus.** A tokenizer can create a token for a string that is frequent in its own data and then hand the model an embedding row that almost never receives a gradient. The model cannot tell you what the token means, because it was never taught.
blocks.section: When the vocabulary is a graveyard: glitch tokens

blocks.quote: This is also a security property. A token the model handles unpredictably is a potential bypass: adversarial tokenization can change a model's behavior or slip text past a classifier that segments it differently (\cite[Geh et al., 2025]{geh2025adversarialtokenization}; \cite[Schulz et al., 2025]{tokenbreak2025}). The lesson for anyone deploying a model is dull but important: **test the tokenizer, not just the model**, and treat “this string is one token” as a claim to verify rather than a guarantee.
blocks.section: When the vocabulary is a graveyard: glitch tokens

blocks.quote: Byte-level: the floor, not the fix
blocks.section: Byte-level: the floor, not the fix

blocks.quote: Byte-level BPE \cite[Radford et al., GPT-2 (2019)]{gpt2} solved the *worst* failure — a token the model cannot even *represent*. Because the alphabet is all 256 bytes, every possible input has a tokenization; there is no unknown token, no "cannot read this script." That is a genuine, large win: a byte-level model can, in principle, read *any* language, including ones it was barely trained on.
blocks.section: Byte-level: the floor, not the fix

blocks.quote: But byte-level does **not** remove the inflation — it only removes the *failure to represent it*. A Thai sentence is still more bytes (hence more tokens) than the same sentence in English, because the information is denser per character in a script with a large alphabet. Byte-level is the **floor**: it guarantees you can tokenize anything. The *relative* cost between languages remains, because it is a property of the languages themselves (how much information per byte), not of the tokenizer's vocabulary.
blocks.section: Byte-level: the floor, not the fix

blocks.quote: The frontier: removing the discrete bottleneck
blocks.section: The frontier: removing the discrete bottleneck

blocks.quote: The current research direction is to shrink, or remove, the discrete-token bottleneck altogether. The clearest first step is **byte-to-byte** pretraining: model over raw bytes rather than over a hand-built subword vocabulary, so there is no per-language vocabulary to be biased by \cite[Xue et al., ByT5 (2022)]{byt52022}. Beyond that, the 2025–26 frontier explores **byte-latent / continuous** representations — learning a continuous "pre-token" space the model predicts over, sidestepping the fixed 256-byte (or fixed-vocabulary) discretization. Whether that actually closes the per-language gap, or merely moves the bias into the continuous representation, is an open question; the honest statement is that the *idea* — stop making a fixed vocabulary the unit of thought — is live and consequential, even where the named systems are not yet settled into stable references you can cite.
blocks.section: The frontier: removing the discrete bottleneck

blocks.quote: The practical takeaway does not depend on the frontier. A tokenizer is a **decision with economic and fairness consequences**, not a detail. If you deploy a model multilingually, the question "how many tokens does a sentence in language *L* cost, relative to the dominant language?" is a real number, it is not one, and it should be measured — because the model's *effective* context window, and its *price*, are different for every language it serves.
blocks.section: The frontier: removing the discrete bottleneck

blocks.quote: The rest of the bestiary
blocks.section: The rest of the bestiary

blocks.quote: Glitch tokens are one member of a family. Once you look at text as *tokens* rather than characters, several other failure modes become visible. None of them is exotic; all of them are consequences of the same decision to cut text at statistically convenient boundaries.
blocks.section: The rest of the bestiary

blocks.quote: Numbers do not survive the trip
blocks.section: Numbers do not survive the trip

blocks.quote: A number is a sequence of digits; a tokenizer sees a string and may group it in ways that depend on frequency rather than place value. `1234` may be one token while `1235` becomes `123` + `5`; a decimal point, a leading zero, or a thousands separator can change the segmentation again. The model then has to do arithmetic across pieces that do not line up with the digits, which is one reason arithmetic accuracy depends on *how the number was written* (\cite[Singh & Strouse, 2024]{singh2024tokenizationcounts}). The fix is not “train harder”; it is to choose a representation that preserves the structure, for example digit-wise tokenization or an external calculator.
blocks.section: Numbers do not survive the trip

blocks.quote: A space is not nothing
blocks.section: A space is not nothing

blocks.quote: Leading and trailing spaces belong to tokens. A prompt ending in `The answer is` and one ending in `The answer is ` can have different next-token distributions, because the final token is different. This matters most at the boundary between a prompt and a generated continuation, where a partial token can force the model into an awkward segmentation. Recent work shows that models can often recover from *non-canonical* tokenizations, but the distribution shift is real and measurable (\cite[Zheng et al., 2025]{zheng2025brokentokens}). Boundary-aware prompting and token healing exist precisely to avoid handing the model a split it did not expect.
blocks.section: A space is not nothing

blocks.quote: One visible character, many tokens
blocks.section: One visible character, many tokens

blocks.quote: Unicode is not a one-to-one mapping from what you see to what the tokenizer receives. The same visible `é` can be one code point or `e` plus a combining acute accent; an emoji can be a single code point or a zero-width-joiner sequence of several; flags, family emoji, and right-to-left text add more cases. Normalization forms (NFC, NFD) can therefore change the token sequence without changing the rendered text (\cite[Unicode Consortium, UAX #15]{unicodeuax15}). Normalize before comparing, classifying, or hashing text — and remember that normalization is itself a lossy decision when the exact byte sequence matters.
blocks.section: One visible character, many tokens

blocks.quote: The same string, a different tokenizer
blocks.section: The same string, a different tokenizer

blocks.quote: Token IDs are not portable. Each model family has its own vocabulary and merge rules, so the same sentence can be longer, shorter, or split at completely different places under a different tokenizer. That is why swapping a tokenizer invalidates the embedding matrix, why token counts from one model are not a budget for another, and why “the context window is 128k tokens” is a statement about a *particular* tokenizer. The tokenizer is part of the model contract, not a preprocessing detail you can change later.
blocks.section: The same string, a different tokenizer

blocks.quote: Spelling, homoglyphs, and filter evasion
blocks.section: Spelling, homoglyphs, and filter evasion

blocks.quote: If a safety filter and a generator tokenize the same text differently, an attacker can exploit the gap: invisible characters, Cyrillic letters that look Latin, leetspeak, or deliberate segmentation can change one side's view while leaving the other's meaning intact. This is the practical face of adversarial tokenization (\cite[Geh et al., 2025]{geh2025adversarialtokenization}; \cite[Schulz et al., 2025]{tokenbreak2025}). Defenses have to normalize and tokenize consistently across every component in the pipeline; a filter that reads characters while the model reads tokens is not protecting the same input.
blocks.section: Spelling, homoglyphs, and filter evasion

blocks.quote: What to do about it
blocks.section: What to do about it

blocks.quote: The pathologies above point to a short engineering checklist:
blocks.section: What to do about it

blocks.quote: > A tokenizer is a lossy interface between text and thought. The loss is not random: it is a set of decisions about which distinctions matter, made before the model sees a single example.
blocks.section: What to do about it

blocks.quote: The next time a model “can't count,” “can't spell,” or “goes weird” on an ordinary-looking string, ask the tokenizer first. It is often the part of the system that made the decision, and the part nobody debugged.
blocks.section: What to do about it
